transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-12-31 10:45 PST (UTC-0800) (2026-12-31T18:45:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 25.288 degrees and its azimuth is 158.346 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 12.474 degrees and its azimuth is 241.521 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 39.99 percent illuminated, 78.295 degrees from the Sun, and 388953.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably yes, but it would be challenging rather than obvious.

At about 40% illumination and 12.5° above the horizon, the Moon is intrinsically bright enough to be visible in daylight. A 78° separation from the Sun is also favorable: you would be looking well away from the Sun, reducing glare and making the sky background less extreme than near the Sun.

The main difficulty is its low altitude. At only ~12° up, atmospheric haze, extinction, and any local obstructions—trees, buildings, distant haze—can substantially reduce contrast. In clear, dry Davis conditions with an unobstructed southwest horizon, an experienced observer who knows the exact direction should have a reasonable chance of finding it. It may look like a faint, washed-out pale patch rather than a crisp Moon.

Your stated azimuth, about 241.5°, is west-southwest. Start there, roughly a fist-width above the horizon (a clenched fist at arm’s length is about 10°), and scan slowly. Avoid looking anywhere near the Sun; it is far to the southeast, so this is not a direct solar-safety issue, but don’t use binoculars or a telescope unless you are completely certain the Sun cannot enter the field.

My honest estimate: **visible under genuinely clear conditions, but easy to miss—perhaps a moderate-to-good chance, around 60–80% if you have a clean horizon and know exactly where to search.**
